blocks.text: Table salt melts at 801 degrees Celsius. Candle wax melts in your hand. Both are solids made of atoms held together, yet one needs a furnace and the other needs body heat. The difference is not the atoms — it is the kind of bond between them.

blocks.markdown:
## Why atoms bond at all

Atoms combine in order to achieve the stable electron arrangement of the nearest noble gas: a **duplet** for the smallest atoms and an **octet** for the rest. There are two main ways to reach it.

- **Transfer** electrons completely: ionic bonding
- **Share** electrons: covalent bonding

Metals have few outer electrons and low ionisation energies, so they lose electrons. Non-metals have nearly full outer shells and high electronegativity, so they gain or share.

blocks.title: Ionic bond
blocks.text: An ionic or electrovalent bond is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the complete transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.

blocks.markdown:
### Ionic bonding: sodium chloride

Sodium is 2, 8, 1 and chlorine is 2, 8, 7.

- Na loses one electron: Na -> Na+ + e-, giving 2, 8
- Cl gains that electron: Cl + e- -> Cl-, giving 2, 8, 8

Overall: 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl

The Na+ and Cl- ions then attract each other in every direction, building a giant three-dimensional **ionic lattice**. There is no such thing as a discrete NaCl molecule in the solid; the formula only gives the ratio.

blocks.title: Covalent bond
blocks.text: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons, with each atom contributing one electron to the pair. In a dative or co-ordinate bond, both electrons of the shared pair come from the same atom, as in NH4+ and H3O+.

blocks.markdown:
### Covalent bonding: some examples

- **H2** — each hydrogen contributes one electron; a single bond gives both a duplet.
- **O2** — each oxygen shares two pairs, forming a double bond so both reach an octet.
- **N2** — three shared pairs form a triple bond, which is why nitrogen is so unreactive.
- **CH4** — carbon shares one electron with each of four hydrogens.
- **CO2** — two double bonds, written O=C=O.

When the two bonded atoms differ in electronegativity, the shared pair is pulled towards the more electronegative atom and the bond is **polar covalent**. HCl is the standard example.

rows: Conducts when molten or in solution
blocks.caption: Properties determined by the type of bonding

blocks.title: Deducing the formula of an ionic compound
blocks.prompt: Element A has atomic number 13 and element B has atomic number 8. Deduce the type of bonding and the formula of the compound they form.

steps.text: Write the electron configurations. A with 13 electrons is 2, 8, 3 and B with 8 electrons is 2, 6.
A has three outer electrons and is a metal, so it loses all three to form A3+. B has six outer electrons and is a non-metal, so it gains two to form B2-.
A metal reacting with a non-metal by transferring electrons means the bonding is ionic.
Balance the charges. The lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6, so two A3+ ions (total +6) pair with three B2- ions (total -6).
The formula is therefore A2B3. With A as aluminium and B as oxygen this is Al2O3, aluminium oxide.

blocks.answer: Ionic bonding, formula A2B3 (aluminium oxide, Al2O3)

blocks.title: Why ionic solids do not conduct but their melts do
blocks.text: Electrical conduction in an ionic compound requires ions that are free to move. In the solid the ions are locked in fixed lattice positions, so no current flows. Melting or dissolving frees the ions, and the liquid conducts. Note that the charge carriers are ions, not electrons as in a metal.

blocks.title: Never say weak covalent bonds
blocks.text: Simple molecular substances have low melting points because the forces between the molecules are weak, not because the covalent bonds are weak. The covalent bonds within each molecule are very strong and stay intact during melting. Examiners penalise the wrong wording heavily.

points: Atoms bond to attain the stable electron arrangement of a noble gas.
Ionic bonding transfers electrons from metal to non-metal and produces a giant lattice of ions.
Covalent bonding shares electron pairs; in a dative bond both electrons come from one atom.
Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct only when molten or dissolved.
Simple covalent substances melt at low temperatures because the forces between molecules, not the bonds within them, are weak.
Giant covalent solids such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have extremely high melting points.
